entries.h: 🩺 Think Like the Nurse — "My back really hurts," right over the costovertebral angle
entries.t: Why does this matter? CVA tenderness means the pain is over the kidney, not the bladder. The infection has ascended — think pyelonephritis, which is a systemic infection that can scar the kidney and seed the bloodstream. ⛔ What assessment should you perform next? Take a full set of vital signs — temperature, HR, BP, RR and mental status — looking for the sepsis picture (fever, HR >100, SBP <100, confusion). Then percuss the CVA gently and check the urine.

entries.h: Clinical Case — Mrs. Wilson, 79, "she just isn't acting like herself"
entries.t: Temp 100.9°F · confused · weak · urinary frequency · BP 100/62 · HR 112 Q1 — What should the nurse suspect FIRST? A urinary tract infection, likely already ascending — and possible early urosepsis. Get a urinalysis with culture, blood cultures, and vitals. Q2 — Why is this different from a younger adult? Older adults often do not mount the classic burning/frequency picture or a high fever. Their presenting sign is a change in mental status — new confusion, falls, incontinence, decreased appetite, or generalized weakness. A "normal" temperature can still be a fever for them because their baseline is lower. Q3 — Which finding makes her higher priority? The combination of HR 112 with BP 100/62 and altered mental status. That is early sepsis physiology — she is compensating now, and a falling BP is next.

Cloudy · nitrites positive · leukocyte esterase positive · WBC elevated · bacteria present · SG 1.025 · trace protein Most likely diagnosis? Bacterial urinary tract infection. Positive nitrites = gram-negative bacteria (usually E. coli ) converting dietary nitrate; positive leukocyte esterase + WBCs = the inflammatory response. Would you expect antibiotics? YES / NO YES — this is a symptomatic bacterial infection. Culture first, then antibiotics. Note SG 1.025 is normal-to-concentrated (normal 1.005–1.030) and trace protein is not alarming here.

1 — Assess pain (assessment before intervention; also tells you whether this is bladder or flank pain) 2 — Obtain urine culture (must be collected BEFORE the first antibiotic dose) 3 — Administer prescribed antibiotic (treat the infection promptly once the specimen is in hand) 4 — Encourage oral fluids (flushes bacteria; supportive, not urgent) 5 — Teach front-to-back wiping (prevention/teaching is always last when someone is acutely ill) Why must the culture come before antibiotics? Even one dose can suppress bacterial growth and give a false-negative culture. Without a positive culture and sensitivities you cannot narrow the antibiotic, so the patient stays on broad-spectrum therapy longer than necessary and resistant organisms get missed. Don't memorize the types — meet the patients. For each one ask: "Why is this patient leaking urine?" Patient A — 42 y/o woman: "Every time I laugh, sneeze, or cough, I leak a little." Type? Stress incontinence WHY? Weak pelvic floor muscles and a weak urethral sphincter, usually after childbirth, aging, or estrogen loss. A cough spikes intra-abdominal pressure above what the sphincter can hold, so a small amount escapes. The bladder itself is normal. First-line treatment? Pelvic floor muscle (Kegel) exercises — plus weight loss, avoiding caffeine/alcohol, and timed voiding. Surgery (sling) and pessaries come later. Patient B — 73 y/o: "When I feel like I have to go, I have about 10 seconds." Type? Urge incontinence (overactive bladder) What is happening inside the bladder? The detrusor muscle contracts involuntarily and too early, before the bladder is actually full — so the urge is sudden, intense, and unstoppable. Nursing intervention? Bladder retraining with a timed voiding schedule, gradually lengthening the interval; cut caffeine, alcohol and artificial sweeteners; keep a path to the toilet clear; anticholinergics such as oxybutynin or tolterodine, or mirabegron, if prescribed. entries.h: Patient C — 82 y/o man with BPH: "I always feel full." Dribbles all day. Bladder scan 850 mL.
entries.t: Type? Overflow incontinence Why? The enlarged prostate obstructs outflow. The bladder over-distends, pressure inside exceeds sphincter resistance, and urine dribbles out over the top — while 850 mL stays behind. Leaking urine does NOT mean the bladder is empty. Priority nursing action? Relieve the retention — bladder scan (done: 850 mL) then catheterize per order. Because that retained volume causes back-pressure → hydronephrosis → postrenal AKI, plus a high infection risk.

entries.h: Patient D — spinal cord injury; bladder empties without warning; no control
entries.t: Type? Reflex incontinence — a neurogenic bladder Why? The spinal cord lesion cuts the communication between bladder and brain. The bladder fills and the reflex arc fires a detrusor contraction at a set volume, with no sensation and no voluntary control. Managed with a scheduled program of intermittent catheterization.

entries.h: Patient E — severe arthritis; can't unbutton pants fast enough
entries.t: Is the bladder working normally? YES / NO YES. The urinary system is intact. Then why is the patient incontinent? This is functional incontinence — a mobility, dexterity, cognition or environment problem, not a bladder problem. Fix the environment: elastic waistbands and Velcro, a bedside commode, a call light within reach, good lighting, clear pathways, and scheduled toileting.

entries.h: Patient F — new incontinence after starting a diuretic; resolves when the drug is adjusted
entries.t: Type? Transient (temporary) incontinence — caused by a reversible trigger. Remember DIAPPERS : Delirium, Infection, Atrophic vaginitis, Pharmaceuticals, Psychological, Excess urine output, Restricted mobility, Stool impaction. 🩺 Think Like a Nurse — Which patient requires the nurse's attention FIRST? Stress incontinence Overflow incontinence with bladder distention Functional incontinence Urge incontinence Show the answer B — Overflow incontinence with bladder distention. Because this one is causing organ damage right now: retained urine raises pressure back up the ureters → hydronephrosis → postrenal AKI, and stagnant urine breeds infection. It is also painful. Bladder scan and catheterize. A, C, D are all quality-of-life problems handled with teaching, retraining and environmental changes. None of them threaten kidney function today.

entries.h: ⛔ Stop & Think — no void in 10 hours, palpable bladder, leaking urine
entries.t: Should the nurse assume the bladder is empty? YES / NO NO. Why? Leaking with a palpable bladder is the classic picture of overflow — the bladder is so full it is spilling. Scan it. If a large residual is present, catheterize per order. Assuming "she's voiding, she's fine" is how retention becomes hydronephrosis. 💡 Clinical Pearl: Overflow incontinence fools students. Leaking urine sometimes means the bladder is too full, not empty. 💬 Ask Claire: "Give me six patient scenarios with different types of urinary incontinence. Do not tell me the diagnosis. Make me identify the type, explain the pathophysiology, and choose the priority nursing intervention."

Lots of urinary problems cause blood in the urine. Bladder cancer is different because of HOW the blood shows up. The classic sign is gross, painless, intermittent hematuria — visibly bloody urine with no burning, no colic, no fever Why is this finding concerning? Painless bleeding means nothing is inflamed, obstructed, or spasming — so infection and stones do not explain it. Untreated bladder cancer keeps growing while the patient feels fine, and the bleeding is intermittent , so people talk themselves out of getting checked when it clears up. Nursing Clue "My urine has blood in it, but it doesn't hurt." The question that should come to mind: "Does this patient smoke, or have they ever?" — and then: painless hematuria in an adult is bladder cancer until proven otherwise. It needs cystoscopy, not reassurance. Risk Factors Risk factor Why does it increase risk? Cigarette smoking The #1 modifiable risk factor. Carcinogens from tobacco are absorbed, filtered by the kidney, and then sit in contact with the bladder lining while urine is stored — a chemical bath on the urothelium. Smokers have roughly 2–4× the risk. Older age Decades of accumulated carcinogen exposure plus age-related DNA repair decline. Most cases are diagnosed after age 55. Risk factor Why does it increase risk? Cigarette smoking The #1 modifiable risk factor. Carcinogens from tobacco are absorbed, filtered by the kidney, and then sit in contact with the bladder lining while urine is stored — a chemical bath on the urothelium. Smokers have roughly 2–4× the risk. Older age Decades of accumulated carcinogen exposure plus age-related DNA repair decline. Most cases are diagnosed after age 55. Male sex Men are diagnosed about 3–4× more often — historically higher smoking and industrial-chemical exposure, plus hormonal differences in the urothelium. Occupational chemical exposure Aromatic amines and dyes — rubber, paint, leather, textile, printing, hairdressing and truck-driving trades. Same mechanism: the chemicals are excreted in urine and pool in the bladder. ⛔ Why do smokers have such a high risk? Because urine is where the body dumps what it detoxifies. What

Test Purpose Urinalysis May detect blood in the urine — often microscopic hematuria; a screening clue, never the diagnosis CT scan Evaluates spread of disease — staging: depth of invasion, nodes, metastasis Cystoscopy Looks directly inside the bladder — the key test; the scope both visualizes and removes tissue Biopsy Confirms the diagnosis — only tissue proves cancer and its grade After cystoscopy, teach: pink-tinged urine and mild burning are expected for a day or two; increase fluids; report bright red bleeding with clots, inability to void, fever, or worsening pain. Priority Question — A patient has gross painless hematuria. What should the nurse do FIRST? Encourage fluids Notify the provider Apply heat Administer antibiotics Show the answer B — Notify the provider. Painless gross hematuria is a red-flag symptom that requires urologic workup (cystoscopy), not a comfort measure. Delay

After the bladder comes out, urine still has to leave the body. The surgeon builds a new road. Draw the arrows — ileal conduit Start Kidney ➜ 1 Ureters ➜ 2 Ileal conduit — a short segment of ileum used as a pipe ➜ 3 Stoma on the abdominal wall ➜ End Collection pouch Key point: an ileal conduit is incontinent and continuous — there is no storage and no sphincter, so urine drains constantly and the pouch is worn 24/7. Expect mucus in the urine; that is normal because the conduit is made of bowel. What Does the Nurse Assess? — circle all that apply Stoma color — ✅ the single most important assessment — it tells you whether the tissue is perfused Skin integrity — ✅ alkaline urine excoriates peristomal skin quickly Urine output — ✅ must be at least ~30 mL/hr; no output = obstruction or hypovolemia Pulse quality — ❌ not a stoma assessment (still part of a general post-op check, just not part of this) Pouch seal — ✅ a leaking seal means skin breakdown and odor within hours Edema around stoma — ✅ mild edema is expected for the first few days; increasing edema is not Healthy or Not? — a stoma should be… ☐ Pale — ❌ suggests anemia or poor perfusion ☐ Black — ❌ necrosis — a surgical emergency ☐ Moist and pink/red — ✅ correct — looks like the inside of your cheek, beefy red and shiny ☐ Dry — ❌ a healthy stoma is always moist; dryness signals compromise 🚨 Critical Thinking — the stoma sudde

entries.h: 🚨 Critical Thinking — the stoma suddenly turns dark purple
entries.t: Priority concern? Impaired blood supply to the stoma — ischemia progressing toward necrosis. Dusky/purple → black means the tissue is dying and the patient needs surgical revision. What should you do FIRST? Notify the surgeon immediately. Ischemic bowel does not recover on its own and cannot be fixed at the bedside. Meanwhile, remove any constricting pouch/belt, do not apply heat or massage, keep the patient NPO in case of a return to the OR, and document the exact color and time.

entries.h: Clinical Judgment — "I have blood in my urine." Five questions before you call the provider
entries.t: 1. Does it hurt? Painless points toward cancer; colicky flank pain points toward a stone; burning points toward infection. 2. When did it start, and is it every void or just at the beginning/end of the stream? Blood throughout suggests a kidney or bladder source. 3. What does it look like — bright red, pink, clots, or cola-colored? Cola/tea colored with edema and hypertension = glomerulonephritis, not bleeding. 4. What else is going on — fever, chills, flank pain, weight loss, trouble voiding? 5. What is your history? Smoking, chemical exposure, anticoagulants, recent procedure or catheter, trauma, strep infection 1–2 weeks ago, beets/rifampin (which just stain the urine). 💙 Dr. K's Clinical Tip Nursing isn't recognizing a disease name. It is asking: Why is this happening? What is the priority? What complication am I trying to prevent? What assessment tells me my patient is getting worse

entries.h: Unit 9 · Glomerulonephritis — When the Filter Becomes Inflamed 🔥
entries.t: Normally: blood enters, waste leaves, protein stays, red cells stay. Now the filter develops tiny holes because it is inflamed. What can now leak through? — circle all that apply □ Water — Water always crosses the filter — that is normal filtration. In GN the problem is that less water gets filtered out, so it is retained. □ Protein — ✅ Yes — but only a moderate amount in GN (usually <3.5 g/day). Massive protein loss belongs to nephrotic syndrome. □ Red blood cells — ✅ Yes — this is the signature. RBCs and RBC casts in the urine turn it cola/tea colored. □ White blood cells — ✅ Yes, WBCs and casts appear because the glomerulus is inflamed. If the kidney filter is inflamed, would urine output increase or decrease? Decrease — oliguria. Explain WHY. Inflammation swells and narrows the glomerular capillary loops, so less plasma is filtered per minute (GFR drops). Less filtrate in = less urine out, and the salt and water that should have been excreted stay in the body → edema and hypertension.

entries.h: Recognizing the Patient — check all that support glomerulonephritis
entries.t: □ Periorbital edema — ✅ Classic — puffy face/eyes on waking, because retained fluid settles in loose tissue overnight □ Cola-colored urine — ✅ The hallmark — RBCs and RBC casts in the urine □ Hypertension — ✅ From sodium and water retention plus RAAS activation □ Proteinuria — ✅ Present, but mild-to-moderate (<3.5 g/day) □ Oliguria — ✅ GFR has fallen □ Weight gain — ✅ Fluid retention — daily weight is the most reliable measure of it Also expect: fatigue and malaise, headache, elevated BUN/creatinine, elevated ASO titer (evidence of recent strep), and low serum complement (C3).

Assessment finding Why does it happen? Edema The damaged glomerulus cannot excrete sodium and water, so volume expands and spills into the interstitium — worst where tissue is loose (around the eyes, in the morning) Hypertension Volume overload plus reduced renal perfusion, which activates RAAS → vasoconstriction and more sodium retention Cola-colored urine Red blood cells leak through the inflamed glomerular membrane; hemoglobin breaks down in acidic urine, turning it brown/tea/cola colored (rather than bright red) Oliguria Inflammation narrows the capillary loops → GFR drops → less filtrate is produced Fatigue Retained uremic wastes, anemia of the inflammatory process, and the work of carrying extra fluid against a high blood pressure NCLEX Pause — Which assessment finding requires immediate follow-up? Blood pressure 188/102 Periorbital edema Cola-colored urine Mild nausea Show the ans

entries.h: 🚨 Clinical Judgment — sudden dyspnea, crackles, SpO₂ 88%
entries.t: What complication is occurring? Acute pulmonary edema from fluid volume overload — the retained fluid has backed up into the lungs. (Circulatory overload can also push into heart failure.) What should the nurse do FIRST? Sit the patient upright in high Fowler's with the legs dependent and apply oxygen. That immediately reduces venous return and lets the diaphragm drop, so it improves oxygenation before any drug can. Then call the provider and anticipate IV furosemide, and keep the patient NPO/fluid-restricted.

Disease Acute glomerulonephritis ➜ Damaged structure The glomerulus — the filtering membrane itself ➜ Major symptoms Cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, hypertension, oliguria, weight gain, fatigue, mild proteinuria ➜ Priority care Blood pressure control, daily weights and strict I&O, sodium and fluid restriction, monitor respiratory status for overload, protein restriction if azotemic, antibiotics if strep is still present, rest 💬 Ask Claire: "Give me five patient scenarios with glomerulonephritis. Help me recognize the disease using only assessment findings. Make me explain WHY every symptom occurs."

entries.h: Unit 10 · Nephrotic Syndrome — When the Filter Leaks Protein 🫧
entries.t: Finish the Story STEP 1 Damaged glomerulus ➜ STEP 2 Protein leaks into urine (>3.5 g/day — massive proteinuria, foamy urine) ➜ STEP 3 Blood loses albumin — and with it, plasma oncotic (pulling) pressure ➜ STEP 4 Fluid leaves the bloodstream ➜ STEP 5 Fluid enters tissues ➜ STEP 6 Massive generalized edema (anasarca) — and because the vascular space is now under-filled, RAAS turns on and retains even more salt and water Why is albumin important? Albumin is a sponge — it pulls water into the bloodstream. If albumin drops, the water leaves the vessels and moves into the interstitial tissue. That is why the swelling is massive yet the intravascular volume can be low: the fluid is in the wrong compartment. Clinical connection: nephrotic edema is not the kidney "making more fluid" — it is fluid leaving the blood vessels. Assessment Detective — which patient has nephrotic syndrome? Patient A (cola-colored urine, hypertension, recent strep) — ❌ That is glomerulonephritis — blood is leaking, and there is a post-infectious trigger. Patient B (foamy urine, +4 pitting edema, albumin 2.1, proteinuria) — ✅ Nephrotic syndrome. Foam = protein in the urine; albumin 2.1 g/dL (normal 3.5–5.0) is the hypoalbuminemia; the +4 edema is the direct consequence of losing oncotic pressure. Fill in the Table Finding Why? Massive edema Low serum albumin → low plasma oncotic pressure → fluid shifts from vess

entries.h: Assessment Detective — which patient has nephrotic syndrome?
entries.t: Patient A (cola-colored urine, hypertension, recent strep) — ❌ That is glomerulonephritis — blood is leaking, and there is a post-infectious trigger. Patient B (foamy urine, +4 pitting edema, albumin 2.1, proteinuria) — ✅ Nephrotic syndrome. Foam = protein in the urine; albumin 2.1 g/dL (normal 3.5–5.0) is the hypoalbuminemia; the +4 edema is the direct consequence of losing oncotic pressure.

Finding Why? Massive edema Low serum albumin → low plasma oncotic pressure → fluid shifts from vessels into tissue; RAAS activation then adds more sodium and water Foamy urine Protein in urine lowers its surface tension, so it froths in the toilet — the patient's own early warning sign Low albumin The damaged glomerular membrane lets albumin escape faster than the liver can replace it Hyperlipidemia The liver senses low oncotic pressure and ramps up production of all its proteins, including lipoproteins — and lipid clearance falls at the same time. Result: high cholesterol, high triglycerides, and lipids in the urine ⛔ Why does the liver make extra cholesterol? It is trying to compensate. The liver's response to falling plasma protein is to synthesize more protein — and lipoprotein synthesis rises along with albumin synthesis. It cannot keep up with the albumin loss, so what you actually

Glomerulonephritis Nephrotic syndrome Blood in urine ✅ Yes — the defining feature. RBCs and RBC casts ❌ Usually minimal or absent Protein in urine Mild to moderate (<3.5 g/day) ✅ Massive (>3.5 g/day) — the defining feature Edema Present but usually mild–moderate; periorbital and facial, worse in the morning Severe and generalized — anasarca, ascites, +3/+4 pitting Hypertension ✅ Common and often severe — volume overload + RAAS Variable; may be normal or even low because the vascular space is under-filled Foamy urine ❌ Not typical ✅ Classic Cola urine ✅ Classic ❌ Not typical Serum albumin Usually near-normal Low — often <3.0 g/dL Lipids Normal High — hyperlipidemia is part of the syndrome Explain this — one sentence for the biggest difference: Glomerulonephritis leaks blood (cola urine + hypertension), nephrotic syndrome leaks protein (foamy urine + massive edema + low albumin).

entries.h: Priority Nursing Care — circle the priorities and say why
entries.t: Monitor blood pressure — ✅ Volume and RAAS shifts move the BP in both directions; ACE inhibitors/ARBs are used specifically to reduce proteinuria Daily weights — ✅ The single best measure of fluid status — 1 kg = 1 L. Same scale, same time, same clothing, after voiding Strict intake/output — ✅ Tells you whether the diuretic is working and whether output is keeping up with intake Assess edema — ✅ Grade and locate it; measure abdominal girth if ascites is present Monitor respiratory status — ✅ The one that outranks the rest — fluid moving into the lungs is the life-threatening turn Monitor albumin — ✅ Tracks severity and response; a rising albumin means the leak is closing Teach low-sodium diet — ✅ Sodium restriction limits the water it drags with it; protein is given at normal, not high, amounts — extra protein just gets spilled and worsens the injury

Weight ↑5 kg · albumin 2.0 · BP 146/88 · lungs clear · +4 edema · urine 4+ protein Q1 — What assessment finding is expected? All of them, actually — the 4+ proteinuria with albumin 2.0 and +4 pitting edema is textbook nephrotic syndrome. The 5 kg gain equals about 5 L of retained fluid. Q2 — What complication is MOST likely if fluid keeps increasing? Pulmonary edema — the lungs are clear now , which is exactly why you keep listening. Pleural effusion, ascites, and worsening skin breakdown follow the same fluid. Q3 — Which intervention best evaluates treatment effectiveness? Daily weight, measured the same way every day. It detects fluid change earlier and more reliably than edema grading or I&O records. 💬 Ask Claire: "Help me compare glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome without memorizing. Use patient cases and ask me why each symptom occurs before giving the answer."

entries.h: 🧠 Pattern Check — answer without looking back
entries.t: Cola-colored urine makes me think: Glomerulonephritis Foamy urine makes me think: Nephrotic syndrome (protein loss) Massive protein loss makes me think: Nephrotic syndrome — and hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, clotting risk Recent strep infection makes me think: Post-infectious acute glomerulonephritis (1–3 weeks later) Periorbital edema is commonly seen in: Both — but it is the classic morning finding of glomerulonephritis, and is part of the generalized edema of nephrotic syndrome The BEST way to monitor fluid status is: Daily weight on the same scale at the same time (1 kg = 1 L of fluid) 💙 Dr. K's Clinical Tip Ask one question: what is leaking through the damaged glomerulus? Blood leaking → glomerulonephritis. Protein leaking → nephrotic syndrome.

Acute means it happened fast — hours to days. The good news: AKI is often reversible if the cause is found and treated early. Where is the problem? Before Blood flow → Prerenal — a perfusion problem; the kidney tissue is still healthy ➜ Inside Kidneys → Intrarenal — damage to the kidney tissue itself (tubules, glomeruli, interstitium) ➜ After Urine leaves kidneys → bladder → urethra → Postrenal — an obstruction anywhere downstream of the kidney AKI Detective — Scenario #1 (83 y/o, 4 days vomiting/diarrhea, BP 82/48, HR 122, dry skin, UOP 12 mL/hr) Are the kidneys damaged? YES / NO NO — not yet. The tissue is intact. Then WHY are they failing? They are not being perfused. GI losses dropped the circulating volume, the MAP fell below what the glomeruli need to filter, and filtration stopped. Fix the volume and the kidney works again — but if the hypoperfusion continues, prerenal AKI becomes acute tubular necrosis, and then it IS damage. 🩺 What do the kidneys need before they can filter? Blood flow. Without perfusion, even perfectly healthy kidneys cannot work. Scenario #2 — IV contrast; creatinine doubles overnight; urine output falls Before / Inside / After? Inside — intrarenal. Explain WHY. Contrast is a nephrotoxin: it constricts renal vessels and is directly toxic to tubular epithelium, producing acute tubular necrosis. The cells slough into the tubules and plug them. Other cl

entries.t: Are the kidneys damaged? YES / NO NO — not yet. The tissue is intact. Then WHY are they failing? They are not being perfused. GI losses dropped the circulating volume, the MAP fell below what the glomeruli need to filter, and filtration stopped. Fix the volume and the kidney works again — but if the hypoperfusion continues, prerenal AKI becomes acute tubular necrosis, and then it IS damage. 🩺 What do the kidneys need before they can filter? Blood flow. Without perfusion, even perfectly healthy kidneys cannot work.

entries.h: Scenario #2 — IV contrast; creatinine doubles overnight; urine output falls
entries.t: Before / Inside / After? Inside — intrarenal. Explain WHY. Contrast is a nephrotoxin: it constricts renal vessels and is directly toxic to tubular epithelium, producing acute tubular necrosis. The cells slough into the tubules and plug them. Other classic intrarenal causes: aminoglycosides, vancomycin, NSAIDs, rhabdomyolysis (myoglobin), transfusion reactions, glomerulonephritis, and prolonged prerenal ischemia.

entries.h: Scenario #3 — severe BPH, no urine for 18 hours, distended bladder, creatinine rising
entries.t: Before / Inside / After? After — postrenal. The prostate is blocking outflow, urine backs up, pressure rises to the kidney, and filtration stops. Healthy kidneys cannot make urine if urine cannot leave. Postrenal AKI is the most rapidly reversible type — if you catch it before the nephrons are destroyed.

Type What's wrong? Examples Prerenal (~60–70%) Not enough blood is reaching the kidney — a perfusion/volume problem. Tissue is intact. BUN:creatinine ratio >20:1; urine is concentrated with low sodium. Hemorrhage, vomiting/diarrhea, burns, dehydration, sepsis (vasodilation), heart failure and cardiogenic shock, anaphylaxis, renal artery stenosis, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors reducing glomerular pressure Intrarenal (~25–40%) The kidney tissue itself is damaged — most often acute tubular necrosis. Urine is dilute (SG near 1.010) with high urine sodium; muddy brown granular casts. IV contrast, aminoglycosides (gentamicin), vancomycin, NSAIDs, chemotherapy, rhabdomyolysis, hemolytic transfusion reaction, acute glomerulonephritis, severe/prolonged ischemia Postrenal (~5–10%) Urine cannot get out. Obstruction → back-pressure → hydronephrosis → filtration stops. Often anuria that alternates with n

entries.h: The Four Phases of AKI — follow the patient
entries.t: PHASE 1 Onset / Initiation — hours to 2 days from the insult until oliguria begins ➜ PHASE 2 Oliguric — 8–14 days; <400 mL/24 hr; the sickest phase ➜ PHASE 3 Diuretic — 1–3 weeks; 1–5+ L/day of dilute urine ➜ PHASE 4 Recovery — GFR climbs back; takes weeks to 12 months Phase 1 — Onset. Write three examples of something that damages the kidneys. 1. A hypotensive event — hemorrhage, sepsis, prolonged surgery, or severe dehydration 2. A nephrotoxin — IV contrast, gentamicin, vancomycin, NSAIDs, or chemotherapy 3. An obstruction — BPH with retention, bilateral stones, or a blocked catheter What assessment finding is MOST important during this phase? Urine output — hourly. A falling output (<0.5 mL/kg/hr or <30 mL/hr) is the earliest sign, and it appears before the creatinine moves. Catching it here is what makes AKI reversible. Phase 2 — Oliguric phase. Fill in the blanks. Urine output becom

entries.h: Clinical Picture — weight gain, +3 edema, crackles, BP 186/98, UOP 180 mL today, K⁺ 6.5
entries.t: What is your FIRST concern? The potassium of 6.5 mEq/L. Put the patient on continuous cardiac monitoring, get a 12-lead, and notify the provider — anticipate IV calcium gluconate (cardiac membrane protection), then insulin + D50 and/or albuterol to shift K⁺ into cells, then sodium polystyrene sulfonate/patiromer or urgent dialysis to remove it. Crackles + 180 mL/day is the close second, and dialysis fixes both.

1 — Monitor ECG (with K⁺ 6.5 this is the assessment that detects lethal change in real time) 2 — Review potassium level (confirms and trends the threat, and guides treatment) 3 — Assess lung sounds (breathing — crackles mean overload has reached the alveoli) 4 — Assess for edema (part of the volume picture, but peripheral edema is not immediately dangerous) 5 — Strict intake and output (essential ongoing monitoring; results accumulate over hours) 6 — Obtain daily weight (the best fluid measure, but it is a once-a-day trend, not a rescue) Which intervention could save the patient's life TODAY? Cardiac monitoring plus acting on the potassium — recognizing peaked T waves and getting calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, and dialysis started.

entries.h: Unit 12 · The Diuretic Phase — The Fluid Management FLIP 🔄
entries.t: Students think: "The patient is peeing again, so they're better." Not so fast. 🩺 Think like the kidney — can they concentrate urine yet? YES / NO NO. The tubules recover their ability to filter before they recover their ability to concentrate . So the patient makes huge volumes of very dilute urine (specific gravity around 1.010) and dumps water and electrolytes they cannot afford to lose. ⭐ The flip — this is the highest-yield concept in AKI Oliguric phase Diuretic phase Urine output <400 mL/24 hr 1–5+ L/day of dilute urine Fluid problem Fluid volume OVERLOAD Fluid volume DEFICIT Potassium HIGH — hyperkalemia LOW — hypokalemia, plus hyponatremia Fluids RESTRICT — usually 24-hr output + ~500–600 mL insensible loss REPLACE — IV/oral fluid and electrolyte replacement Watch for Pulmonary edema, hypertension, lethal dysrhythmia from high K⁺ Hypotension, dehydration, hypovolemic shock, dysrhythmia from LOW K⁺, falls Diet Restrict potassium, sodium, phosphorus and protein Liberalize — potassium is now being replaced, not restricted Same patient, same disease, opposite orders. The exam loves this. Daily weight — ✅ Now you are watching for weight LOSS that is too fast — more than ~0.5–1 kg/day means over-diuresis Blood pressure — ✅ Hypotension is the expected danger of this phase Potassium — ✅ It flipped — now the risk is hypokalemia; check for flat T waves, U waves, weak muscles, ileus Intake and output — ✅ Output can exceed intake by liters; replacement is calculated from these numbers Fall precautions — ✅ Weak, hypotensive, dizzy patient making frequent urgent trips to the bathroom — a fall waiting to happen Orthostatic blood pressure — ✅ The earliest objective sign of volume depletion — a drop of ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic on standing 🩺 Your patient made 5 liters of urine today. Celebrate or assess? Assess. Five liters is not recovery, it is a fluid and electrolyte emergency in slow motion. Check BP and orthostatics, HR, weight change, mucous membranes and skin tur

How long? Weeks to months — sometimes up to a year. GFR climbs back toward baseline, but some patients are left with a permanently reduced GFR and go on to develop CKD. Reflection — why is AKI potentially reversible while CKD is not? In AKI the nephrons are stunned or acutely injured, not gone — tubular cells can regenerate once the cause (low perfusion, toxin, obstruction) is removed. In CKD the nephrons are progressively destroyed and replaced by fibrous scar tissue, and nephrons do not regenerate . Treatment in CKD slows the loss; it does not restore it. Client A: Potassium 6.8, telemetry shows peaked T waves Client B: Creatinine 5.2, urine output 400 mL/day Client C: BP 168/88, weight gain 2 pounds Client D: BUN 54, complains of fatigue Show the answer A — Potassium 6.8 with peaked T waves. entries.h: Unit 13 · Chronic Kidney Disease — The Kidneys Are Tired 🏭
entries.t: 100 workers in a factory. One quits, the other 99 work harder. Then another. Then another. Eventually there aren't enough workers left to run the factory. That is CKD. Build the Story STEP 1 Healthy kidneys ➜ STEP 2 Some nephrons become damaged ➜ STEP 3 Remaining nephrons work harder — they hyperfiltrate to compensate, which is why labs stay normal for years… and that overwork eventually destroys them too ➜ STEP 4 More damage occurs ➜ STEP 5 GFR decreases — progressively and permanently ➜ STEP 6 Waste products accumulate — azotemia, then uremia when symptoms appear ➜ STEP 7 Kidneys can no longer maintain homeostasis ➜ STEP 8 End-Stage Kidney Disease Remember: CKD is progressive and irreversible — treatment slows progression, it does not cure. Definition: kidney damage or GFR <60 mL/min for 3 months or longer . Why do people develop CKD? — which chronic diseases damage blood vessels? □ Diabetes — ✅ #1 cause. Chronic hyperglycemia thickens and scars the glomerular capillaries (diabetic nephropathy). Earliest sign: microalbuminuria. □ Hypertension — ✅ #2 cause. High pressure sclerose the small renal arterioles — and the damaged kidney then raises BP further, a vicious cycle. □ Lupus — ✅ Yes — lupus nephritis is immune-complex damage to the glomerulus □ Recurrent kidney infections — ✅ Yes — repeated pyelonephritis scars renal tissue permanently □ Polycystic kidney disease — ✅ Yes —

entries.h: Why do people develop CKD? — which chronic diseases damage blood vessels?
entries.t: □ Diabetes — ✅ #1 cause. Chronic hyperglycemia thickens and scars the glomerular capillaries (diabetic nephropathy). Earliest sign: microalbuminuria. □ Hypertension — ✅ #2 cause. High pressure sclerose the small renal arterioles — and the damaged kidney then raises BP further, a vicious cycle. □ Lupus — ✅ Yes — lupus nephritis is immune-complex damage to the glomerulus □ Recurrent kidney infections — ✅ Yes — repeated pyelonephritis scars renal tissue permanently □ Polycystic kidney disease — ✅ Yes — the leading inherited cause; cysts replace functioning nephrons 🩺 Which two diseases cause MOST cases, and why? Diabetes and hypertension — together roughly two-thirds of all CKD. Both are diseases of the blood vessels , and the kidney is essentially a filter made of a million tiny blood vessels. Whatever damages vessels systemically damages nephrons. This is also why BP and glucose control a

entries.h: Stages of CKD — understand the trend
entries.t: Stage GFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) What is happening? Stage 1 >90 Kidney damage present (protein in the urine, or an abnormal scan) but normal GFR. Patient feels fine. Focus: treat the cause — glucose and BP control, stop nephrotoxins. Stage 2 60–89 (mild ↓) Mild loss with damage. Still usually asymptomatic. Estimate progression rate and keep protecting the kidney. Stage 3 (3a 45–59 / 3b 30–44) 30–59 (moderate ↓↓) The turning point — labs finally change. Creatinine and BUN rise; anemia, hyperphosphatemia and early bone disease begin. Start dietary restrictions, phosphate binders, ESAs, and adjust drug doses. Stage 4 15–29 (severe ↓↓↓) Overt uremia. Prepare for renal replacement therapy — education about dialysis choices, transplant referral, and placement of an AV fistula now so it has months to mature. Stage 5 <15 End-stage kidney disease. The kidneys cannot sustain life. Dialysis or transplant

entries.h: Body System Challenge — CKD affects almost EVERY system. Why?
entries.t: System Finding → Why? 🧠 Brain Confusion. Uremic toxins cross into the CNS — uremic encephalopathy. Add anemia (less O₂ delivery) and electrolyte shifts. Progresses from foggy → lethargic → seizures. Peripheral neuropathy and restless legs come from the same toxins. ❤️ Heart Hypertension. Sodium and water retention expands volume, and the damaged kidney over-secretes renin → RAAS → vasoconstriction and aldosterone. The hypertension then damages the kidney further. Long term: LVH, heart failure, and — in late uremia — pericarditis with a friction rub. 🫁 Lungs Crackles. Fluid the kidney cannot excrete backs up into the pulmonary circulation → pulmonary edema. Kussmaul respirations also appear as the lungs try to compensate for metabolic acidosis. 🩸 Blood Anemia. Damaged kidneys make less erythropoietin , so the marrow gets no signal to produce RBCs. entries.h: Which Finding Worries You Most? — rank 1 (highest) to 5
entries.t: 1 — Potassium 6.4 (cardiac arrest risk in minutes — get an ECG) 2 — Calcium 7.8 (hypocalcemia → tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, prolonged QT — the second value with an acute neuromuscular/cardiac threat) 3 — Hemoglobin 8.5 (impairs oxygen delivery now; symptomatic, but treated over days–weeks with ESAs and iron) 4 — Creatinine 5.8 (tells you the severity of the disease; not directly dangerous) 5 — Phosphorus 6.2 (drives long-term bone disease and itching — a months-to-years problem; treat with binders taken WITH meals) Explain your ranking: Rank by how fast the value can kill. Electrolytes that change cardiac membrane excitability come first (potassium, then calcium), then oxygen-carrying capacity, then markers of severity, then chronic complications.

entries.h: The Nursing Process — what will you monitor every shift?
entries.t: ☐ Weight — ✅ Best single fluid indicator — same scale, same time, after voiding ☐ Lung sounds — ✅ Crackles are the earliest sign that overload reached the alveoli ☐ Intake/output — ✅ Guides the fluid restriction and shows whether they are still making urine ☐ Potassium — ✅ The lab with the shortest fuse ☐ Blood pressure — ✅ Both cause and consequence of kidney damage; control slows progression ☐ Mental status — ✅ New confusion = rising uremic toxins, or a dangerous electrolyte shift ☐ Skin — ✅ Itching, dryness, bruising and breakdown; edematous skin tears easily ☐ Edema — ✅ Grade and locate; check the sacrum in bedbound patients, not just ankles Why are daily weights one of the BEST assessments in CKD? Because 1 kg of weight change = 1 liter of fluid , and weight detects fluid shifts before edema is visible or crackles are audible. I&O records get missed and edema grading is subjective —

entries.h: Clinical Judgment Case — Mr. Lopez, dialysis tomorrow
entries.t: Weight ↑4 kg since last treatment · BP 192/102 · bibasilar crackles · +3 edema · K⁺ 6.3 · SpO₂ 90% Q1 — What concerns you MOST? Two findings are competing: the potassium of 6.3 and the SpO₂ of 90% with crackles. Assess the breathing first (ABCs — sit him up and give oxygen), but the potassium is the finding that will kill him fastest, so get the ECG and call immediately. Both point to the same answer: he needs dialysis today , not tomorrow. Q2 — What complication is developing? Fluid volume overload with pulmonary edema (4 kg = ~4 L retained), plus severe hyperkalemia — the classic missed-or-inadequate-dialysis picture. Q3 — What order would you anticipate? Urgent/emergent hemodialysis — it removes the fluid and the potassium at the same time. Also expect oxygen, IV calcium gluconate + insulin/dextrose to buy time on the potassium, and possibly IV furosemide if he still makes urine. Q4 —

entries.h: Unit 15 · Dialysis — When the Kidneys Can't Do Their Job Anymore 🩸
entries.t: Dialysis does not fix the kidneys. It takes over some of their jobs — not all of them. What can dialysis actually do? Kidney function Can dialysis do it? So what? Remove excess fluid ✅ YES — by ultrafiltration This is why weight drops during treatment; "dry weight" is the target Remove waste products ✅ YES — urea and creatinine diffuse across the membrane BUN and creatinine fall after each treatment Remove potassium ✅ YES Dialysis is the definitive treatment for hyperkalemia in ESRD Correct acid–base imbalance ✅ YES — bicarbonate in the dialysate buffers the acidosis pH and HCO₃⁻ improve after treatment Produce erythropoietin ❌ NO — that is a hormone the kidney makes , not a solute it removes Which is why dialysis patients still need epoetin alfa and iron Activate vitamin D ❌ NO — also a manufacturing job, not a filtering job Which is why they still need calcitriol and phosphate binders, and still get bone disease 🩺 Why does a dialysis patient still have anemia? Because dialysis is a filter , not an organ . It can subtract things from the blood but it cannot secrete erythropoietin, so the marrow still gets no signal. Blood loss in the dialyzer circuit and frequent lab draws make it worse. Why might they still have weak bones? Same reason — dialysis cannot activate vitamin D. entries.h: Clinical Reasoning — who benefits from peritoneal dialysis?
entries.t: □ Lives several hours from a dialysis center — ✅ PD is done at home, so no thrice-weekly travel □ Wants more independence — ✅ Self-managed, flexible schedule, fewer dietary restrictions □ Has severe cardiovascular instability — ✅ The slow, continuous fluid removal avoids the abrupt volume shifts and hypotension that hemodialysis causes — much better tolerated by an unstable heart ⚠️ Who should NOT get PD? Patients with extensive abdominal adhesions or prior extensive abdominal surgery, active abdominal infection or peritonitis, hernias, severe obesity, or anyone who cannot maintain sterile technique at home.

entries.h: Unit 15b · Peritoneal Dialysis — What Should Normal Look Like? 🚨
entries.t: STEP 1 — FILL Warmed dialysate infuses by gravity into the peritoneal cavity (~10 min) ➜ STEP 2 — DWELL Fluid sits; waste, K⁺ and water move across the peritoneum into the dialysate ➜ STEP 3 — DRAIN Bag lowered below the abdomen; effluent drains out by gravity ⚠️ Warm the dialysate with a dry heating pad or warmer — never in a microwave . Cold fluid causes pain and cramping; overheated fluid burns the peritoneum. Assessment Expected finding Drainage color Clear, pale yellow — like straw. (Slightly blood-tinged is acceptable only in the first few exchanges after catheter insertion.) Catheter site Clean, dry and intact — no redness, warmth, swelling, tenderness or purulent drainage Outflow amount Equal to or greater than the amount infused — that difference is the fluid being removed. Outflow less than inflow means retained fluid: reposition the patient, check for kinks and constipation, and keep the bag below the abdomen. Temperature Normal — afebrile. Any fever in a PD patient is peritonitis until proven otherwise. Abdomen Mild fullness/pressure during dwell is expected. Rebound tenderness, rigidity and severe pain are not. Blood glucose May run high — dialysate contains dextrose, which is absorbed. Expected, especially in diabetics; monitor glucose. ⛔ STOP — the dialysate suddenly becomes cloudy First thought? PERITONITIS — cloudy effluent is the earliest and most reliable sig

entries.h: ⛔ STOP — the dialysate suddenly becomes cloudy
entries.t: First thought? PERITONITIS — cloudy effluent is the earliest and most reliable sign, and it usually appears before the fever. Why is this an emergency? The peritoneum is a huge, highly vascular surface with a catheter running straight into it from the outside. Infection there spreads to the bloodstream fast (sepsis), and repeated episodes scar the membrane so PD stops working permanently. Send effluent for cell count, Gram stain and culture, then give antibiotics — often added directly into the dialysate.

entries.h: Recognizing Peritonitis — circle every finding that concerns you
entries.t: □ Fever — ✅ Systemic infection □ Cloudy drainage — ✅ The hallmark and the earliest sign □ Clear yellow drainage — ❌ That is the normal, expected finding □ Abdominal pain — ✅ Diffuse pain with rebound tenderness — the peritoneum is inflamed □ Chills — ✅ Rigors point to bacteremia □ Redness around catheter — ✅ Exit-site infection — the usual doorway for peritonitis □ Bloody drainage — ✅ Concerning after the first few post-insertion exchanges — report it 🩺 Which finding should you report FIRST? The cloudy dialysate with abdominal pain — together they are diagnostic of peritonitis, and they show up before the patient looks septic. Report immediately and send the effluent for culture. entries.h: Unit 15c · Hemodialysis & Vascular Access — Your Lifeline 🩸
entries.t: Without vascular access, there is no dialysis. Match the Access Device Access What it is Advantage Watch out AV fistula A surgeon connects the patient's own artery directly to a vein (usually radial artery to cephalic vein), and the vein enlarges and toughens Best long-term option — lowest infection and clotting rates, lasts the longest because it is all native tissue Needs 6 weeks to 4 months to mature before it can be used — so it must be placed well before dialysis is needed (stage 4) AV graft A synthetic tube is tunneled to join an artery and a vein when the patient's own vessels are too small or damaged Usable much sooner — about 2–4 weeks — and an option when native veins are inadequate Higher clotting and infection risk than a fistula, because it is foreign material Central venous catheter A large-bore catheter placed in the internal jugular or subclavian vein Can be used immediately — the choice for emergent dialysis or as a bridge while a fistula matures Highest infection risk of all (direct line to the central circulation) plus thrombosis and central vein stenosis — it is a temporary solution. Do not use the dialysis catheter for routine IV fluids or blood draws unless specifically permitted. entries.h: Assessment Detective — your patient has an AV fistula
entries.t: I should FEEL a THRILL — a buzzing/purring vibration under your fingertips (palpate) I should HEAR a BRUIT — a swishing, whooshing sound with the bell of the stethoscope (auscultate) What if they're missing? The access is clotted or occluded. Also check for a cool, pale, numb or painful hand distal to the fistula — that is steal syndrome, where the fistula is diverting blood away from the hand. What does no thrill mean? Blood is not flowing through the fistula — it has thrombosed. Without it, the patient has no way to receive dialysis. What should the nurse do? Notify the provider/dialysis team immediately — a clotted access is a time-sensitive problem; declotting or thrombectomy may still save it. Meanwhile protect the arm: no BP, no sticks, no constriction, and document the exact time you last felt a thrill.

entries.h: ❌ Protect the Access! — circle ALL actions that are NOT allowed
entries.t: Blood pressure on that arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — the cuff compresses the fistula and can clot it IV insertion in that arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — punctures introduce infection and damage the vessel Blood draws from that arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — same reason; use the other arm Palpate for thrill — ✅ Allowed — required, in fact, every shift Listen for bruit — ✅ Allowed — also required every shift Sleep on the access arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — hours of body weight on it can occlude it Carry heavy groceries with that arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — heavy lifting and pressure compromise flow Wear tight clothing or jewelry on that arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — anything constricting, including a watch or tight sleeve Explain WHY: Anything that compresses, punctures, or constricts the access can clot it — and if the access clots, the patient loses the treatment that keeps them alive. Post a sign at the bedside and teach the patient

entries.h: Before Dialysis — check all that apply
entries.t: ☐ Weight — ✅ Pre-weight vs. dry weight determines how much fluid to pull off ☐ Blood pressure — ✅ Baseline for detecting the hypotension that fluid removal causes ☐ Potassium — ✅ Drives urgency and dialysate composition ☐ Medication list — ✅ Some drugs must be held; some must be redosed after ☐ Lung sounds — ✅ Baseline volume status ☐ Access site — ✅ Thrill, bruit, and signs of infection — no access, no treatment Which medications are commonly held before dialysis? Antihypertensives (and often other BP-lowering drugs), plus water-soluble medications that dialysis will simply remove — many antibiotics, water-soluble vitamins, and digoxin needs special attention. Why? Dialysis itself drops the blood pressure by pulling off several liters of fluid. Giving an antihypertensive first stacks two BP-lowering effects and causes symptomatic hypotension mid-treatment. entries.h: During Dialysis — the blood pressure suddenly drops
entries.t: Why might this happen? Fluid is being removed from the vascular space faster than it can refill from the tissues → hypovolemia. Made worse by taking antihypertensives beforehand, eating during treatment (blood shunts to the gut), too aggressive an ultrafiltration goal, or an inaccurate dry weight. Also consider bleeding from the access and, rarely, a transfusion-type or air-embolism reaction. What assessment should you perform FIRST? Recheck the blood pressure and assess the patient's level of consciousness and symptoms (dizziness, nausea, cramping, pallor, diaphoresis). Then lower the head of the bed / Trendelenburg, slow or stop ultrafiltration, and give a normal saline bolus per protocol to restore volume.

entries.h: After Dialysis — what do you expect?
entries.t: Parameter Expected finding Weight ↓ DECREASED — typically 1–4 kg, matching the liters of fluid removed. This is the main measure of treatment effectiveness. Blood pressure ↓ DECREASED — watch for symptomatic hypotension and orthostasis Potassium ↓ DECREASED — back toward normal (sometimes low enough to matter, so recheck) BUN ↓ DECREASED Creatinine ↓ DECREASED — though not to normal; it rises again before the next treatment Hemoglobin Essentially unchanged or slightly lower — dialysis does not treat anemia and some blood is lost in the circuit Nursing priority — the FIRST thing you assess after dialysis? Vital signs , especially blood pressure, plus weight — hypotension from rapid fluid removal is the most common post-dialysis complication. Then check the access site for bleeding (they were heparinized) and confirm the thrill and bruit are still present. Hold pressure, do not massage, if

entries.h: Complications — match the complication to its cause
entries.t: Complication Cause What you do Hypotension Rapid removal of fluid — the vascular space empties faster than it can refill Trendelenburg, slow/stop ultrafiltration, saline bolus per protocol, recheck BP Disequilibrium syndrome Rapid movement of water into brain cells — urea is cleared from the blood faster than from the CNS, so water follows the osmotic gradient into the brain → cerebral edema Slow or stop dialysis and notify the provider — prevented by short, slow initial treatments Access infection Redness, warmth, drainage — organisms entering at the needle/catheter site Culture, antibiotics, strict aseptic technique; systemic infection can seed heart valves Access clotting No thrill or bruit — thrombosis, usually after compression, hypotension, or a BP cuff on that arm Notify immediately — declotting/thrombectomy is time-sensitive Muscle cramps Rapid fluid and electrolyte shifts during

entries.h: ⛔ STOP & THINK — nausea → headache → confusion during dialysis
entries.t: What complication comes to mind? Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome. The classic progression is nausea → headache → restlessness → confusion → twitching → seizures. Most common during the first few treatments or when the BUN was very high. Why is this dangerous? It is cerebral edema. Urea leaves the blood quickly but lingers in brain tissue, so water is pulled into brain cells. Untreated it progresses to seizures, coma and death. Slow or stop the dialysis and notify the provider now.

entries.h: Clinical Judgment Case — Mr. Adams returns from dialysis
entries.t: BP 88/52 · HR 112 · dizzy · weight down 3 kg · AV fistula dressing dry Q1 — Why is his blood pressure low? Three liters of fluid were removed from his vascular space in a few hours (3 kg = 3 L). The intravascular volume dropped faster than fluid could shift back in from the tissues → hypovolemia, with the HR of 112 as the compensation. Q2 — What should the nurse do FIRST? Lie him flat and elevate his legs (or place in Trendelenburg) — it returns blood to the central circulation immediately and costs nothing. Then recheck BP and HR, keep him in bed, and notify the provider; anticipate a small normal saline bolus and reevaluation of his dry weight. Q3 — Should he stand up quickly? YES / NO NO. He is hypovolemic and orthostatic — standing quickly will drop his cerebral perfusion and cause syncope and a fall. Change positions slowly, dangle first, and assist with ambulation; fall precautions

entries.h: Compare These Patients — rank 1 (highest priority) to 4
entries.t: Patient D — K⁺ 6.8 with peaked T waves awaiting dialysis. #1 — lethal dysrhythmia possible within minutes; the ECG proves the heart is already affected. Patient A — Cloudy PD drainage, temp 101.9°F. #2 — peritonitis heading toward sepsis; needs cultures and antibiotics within the hour. Patient C — BP 86/48 after dialysis, dizzy when upright. #3 — a real perfusion problem and a fall risk, but it responds immediately to positioning and fluid. Patient B — No thrill over AV fistula. #4 — urgent (the access may be lost and dialysis delayed), but it is not killing anyone in the next ten minutes. Reasoning: Rank by ABCs and by what kills fastest: a lethal rhythm now > an infection becoming sepsis in hours > hypotension that you can fix at the bedside > loss of access that threatens the next treatment. A transplant is life-changing — but it is not a cure. The body sees the new kidney as foreign and will try to attack it. ⛔ Stop & Think If your immune system attacks the new kidney, what is this called? Rejection. Hyperacute occurs within minutes to 48 hours (the organ must be removed); acute occurs within about the first week to 3 months and is often treatable; chronic occurs over months to years and gradually destroys the graft. How do we prevent it? Careful donor–recipient matching (ABO and HLA, plus a crossmatch) and lifelong immunosuppressant therapy — typically a calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine or tacrolimus) + an antiproliferative (mycophenolate) + a corticosteroid. Build the Story 1 Healthy donor kidney ➜ 2 Surgery — the new kidney is placed in the iliac fossa (lower abdomen); the old kidneys usually stay in ➜ 3 Body recognizes new kidney as foreign ➜ 4 Immune system mounts an attack against the graft (rejection) ➜ 5 Patient must take immunosuppressants for life What if they stop taking them? The immune system reactivates and rejects the graft — the kidney fails and the patient goes back on dialysis, having burned a scarce organ. Nonadherence is one of the leading causes of late graft loss, so assess for cost barriers, side effects (hirsutism, gum overgrowth, tremor, weight gain, mood changes) and understanding at every visit. entries.h: Nursing Priorities after Kidney Transplant — check them off
entries.t: ☐ Monitor urine output — ✅ The #1 indicator of graft function. Hourly at first; a sudden decrease is an early sign of rejection or of obstruction/thrombosis. ☐ Monitor for infection — ✅ Immunosuppression makes infection the leading cause of death after transplant — and the signs are blunted ☐ Encourage medication adherence — ✅ Lifelong, on schedule, never skipped — missed doses cost the kidney ☐ Teach low-sodium diet — ✅ Supports blood pressure control and protects the new kidney (steroids also cause sodium retention) ☐ Assess incision — ✅ Steroids and immunosuppressants delay healing and mask redness; watch for dehiscence and leakage ☐ Encourage incentive spirometer — ✅ Prevents atelectasis and pneumonia — a critical concern when the immune system is suppressed ☐ Monitor creatinine — ✅ A rising creatinine is one of the earliest laboratory signs of rejection ☐ Monitor temperature — ✅ Eve

entries.h: Why Are Transplant Patients So Vulnerable?
entries.t: Immunosuppressants decrease the body's ability to mount an immune response — to recognize and fight invading organisms and abnormal cells This places the patient at risk for infection (bacterial, viral — CMV, BK virus, herpes — and fungal), reactivation of latent infections such as TB, and long-term malignancy , especially skin cancer and lymphoma. Teach: avoid crowds and sick contacts, meticulous hand hygiene, no live vaccines, food safety, daily sunscreen, and report ANY fever right away.

Teach the client to avoid: ☐ Milk — ❌ Not a concern ☐ Grapefruit juice — ✅ AVOID. ☐ Bananas — ❌ Not related to cyclosporine (relevant to potassium counseling instead) ☐ Cranberry juice — ❌ Not a concern for this drug Why? Grapefruit inhibits the CYP3A4 enzyme that metabolizes cyclosporine, so drug levels climb into the toxic range → nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, tremor, hypertension and severe over-immunosuppression. The same warning applies to tacrolimus. Also teach: take at the same time every day, do not skip doses, expect gum overgrowth (see the dentist and brush meticulously) and hirsutism, and have trough levels drawn as ordered. NCLEX Priority — A kidney transplant recipient calls the clinic. Which statement requires immediate follow-up? "I've gained two pounds." "I have a temperature of 100.8°F." "I'm drinking lots of water." "I'm walking every day." Show the answer B — "I have

entries.h: Unit 17 · Polycystic Kidney Disease — When Cysts Replace Healthy Kidneys 🧬
entries.t: Not an infection. Not a lifestyle disease. It is inherited — most commonly autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance. Big Picture 1 Healthy nephrons ➜ 2 Fluid-filled cysts develop ➜ 3 Kidneys enlarge ➜ 4 Healthy tissue is replaced ➜ 5 Kidney function progressively declines → CKD → end-stage renal disease, usually by age 50–60 What Makes PKD Different? As cysts grow they squeeze the tiny vessels inside the kidney. What happens when blood flow decreases? The juxtaglomerular cells sense low renal perfusion — exactly as they would in hemorrhage — and switch on the RAAS. So the kidneys release: RENIN → angiotensin I → (ACE) angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor → aldosterone, which retains sodium and water; ADH is released too. What happens next? Blood pressure RISES — and the hypertension then damages the remaining nephrons, which further reduces perfusion, which releases more renin. A self-feeding loop. ⭐ Dr. K's Clinical Tip: the hypertension in PKD is not stress — it is RAAS activation caused by cysts compressing renal blood vessels, and it is one of the most tested concepts in this unit. Pattern Recognition Finding Why does it happen? Hypertension Cysts compress renal vessels → the kidney reads it as hypoperfusion → renin → RAAS → vasoconstriction + sodium/water retention. Present in most patients before the GFR even falls. Enlarged abdomen The

Finding Why does it happen? Hypertension Cysts compress renal vessels → the kidney reads it as hypoperfusion → renin → RAAS → vasoconstriction + sodium/water retention. Present in most patients before the GFR even falls. Enlarged abdomen The kidneys can grow to many times normal size and become palpable bilaterally — abdominal fullness, early satiety, and a visibly protuberant abdomen Flank pain Stretching of the renal capsule by enlarging cysts, or pressure on surrounding structures — a dull, chronic ache Hematuria A cyst ruptures into the collecting system, or a stone passes — bleeding into the urine, often with a sudden increase in pain Kidney stones Distorted anatomy causes urinary stasis, and the concentrating defect makes urine more lithogenic — roughly 20–30% of patients form stones Progressive kidney failure Every cyst that expands destroys the functioning nephrons around it. Los

Dull, aching flank pain — Chronic pain from enlarging cysts stretching the renal capsule. Expected; managed with heat and non-nephrotoxic analgesia. Sharp, severe flank pain — Something acute: a ruptured cyst , a kidney stone , or an infected cyst. Look for new hematuria, fever, and hypotension — and report it.

entries.h: 🩺 Why is blood pressure the MOST important thing to monitor in PKD?
entries.t: Because controlling blood pressure is the one intervention that measurably slows the loss of kidney function. Uncontrolled hypertension accelerates nephron destruction, and PKD patients also carry a high rate of cerebral (berry) aneurysms — a hypertensive crisis can rupture one. So BP control protects both the kidneys and the brain. ACE inhibitors/ARBs are first line.

entries.h: Nursing Priorities — rank highest to lowest
entries.t: 1 — Monitor blood pressure (the intervention that changes the disease trajectory and prevents aneurysm rupture) 2 — Monitor renal labs (creatinine, BUN, GFR, K⁺ — detects decline and dangerous electrolytes) 3 — Assess pain (comfort, and a change in the pain pattern signals rupture, stone or infection) 4 — Monitor daily weights (fluid status as function declines) 5 — Encourage low-sodium diet (essential long-term teaching that supports BP control — but teaching ranks below monitoring an unstable parameter) Reasoning: Assessment and monitoring of the parameter that can cause acute harm come before comfort measures, and long-term teaching always ranks last on a priority list.

entries.h: 🚨 Clinical Judgment — worsening headaches, blurred vision, BP 198/112
entries.t: What complication concerns you most? A hypertensive emergency — and specifically, in PKD, rupture of a cerebral (berry) aneurysm or hypertensive encephalopathy/stroke. Headache + visual changes + a diastolic over 110 is end-organ damage in progress. What should the nurse do FIRST? Notify the provider immediately and prepare for rapid, controlled BP reduction. Because this pressure is actively damaging the brain, eyes and kidneys right now. Meanwhile: keep the patient quiet with the head of bed elevated, do a neuro check, recheck the BP in both arms, and have seizure precautions and IV access ready. 💬 Ask Claire: "Help me understand polycystic kidney disease by connecting every symptom back to the growing cysts. Quiz me on why blood pressure control is the highest priority and how untreated hypertension accelerates kidney damage."

Blowing up balloons inside a sponge. At first the sponge still works — but as more balloons grow, there isn't much sponge left. Build the Story 1 Inherited genetic disorder ➜ 2 Fluid-filled cysts develop ➜ 3 Healthy nephrons become compressed and destroyed — replaced by cyst and scar tissue ➜ 4 Kidneys become enlarged — often massively, and palpable ➜ 5 Blood flow through the kidneys decreases ➜ 6 Blood pressure increases — via renin/RAAS ➜ 7 Kidney function gradually declines ➜ 8 Progressive kidney (renal) failure ⛔ Stop & Think — is PKD acute, chronic, congenital, or infectious? ☐ Acute — ❌ It develops over decades, not hours ☐ Chronic — ✅ Yes — slowly progressive and irreversible ☐ Congenital — ✅ Yes — the genetic defect is present from birth (inherited), even though symptoms usually appear in the 30s–40s ☐ Infectious — ❌ Not caused by an organism — though cysts can become infected as a complication 🩺 PKD develops over many years. Why don't patients get sick immediately? Because the kidney has enormous reserve. The undamaged nephrons hyperfiltrate and compensate, so labs and blood pressure stay normal until roughly half of function is gone. Symptoms typically surface between ages 30 and 40, and the first sign is usually hypertension — which is why family screening and early BP control matter so much. entries.h: Why Is Blood Pressure So Important? — complete the pathway
entries.t: 1 Growing cysts ➜ 2 Compress renal blood vessels ➜ 3 Kidneys receive less blood flow / perfusion (oxygenated blood) ➜ 4 Kidneys think blood pressure is too LOW ➜ 5 RAAS is activated ➜ 6 Blood pressure increases — vasoconstriction plus sodium and water retention ➜ 7 Kidney damage accelerates — and the cycle repeats Clinical connection — why is BP control the top nursing priority? Because it is the only modifiable factor that slows the disease. Every year of uncontrolled hypertension destroys nephrons faster and moves the patient closer to dialysis, and it also raises the risk of rupturing a cerebral aneurysm. Think of hypertension as fuel on the fire.

entries.h: Recognizing the Patient — check each expected finding
entries.t: ☐ Flank pain — ✅ Dull and chronic from capsular stretch ☐ Enlarged abdomen — ✅ Bilaterally palpable, massively enlarged kidneys ☐ Hypertension — ✅ Usually the earliest sign of all ☐ Bloody urine — ✅ Gross or microscopic hematuria from cyst rupture ☐ Kidney stones — ✅ Common — urinary stasis and concentrated urine ☐ Constipation — ✅ Yes — the enlarged kidneys physically press on the bowel ☐ Progressive fatigue — ✅ From rising uremic toxins and anemia as function declines ☐ Frequent hypoglycemia — ❌ Not a feature of PKD. (Late kidney disease actually reduces insulin clearance, but hypoglycemia is not a recognized PKD finding.) Extra-renal cysts and complications to know: liver cysts (most common), plus pancreatic and splenic cysts, cerebral berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, and colonic diverticula.

entries.h: Which Pain Is It? — part two
entries.t: "My side has been aching for weeks." — ☐ Enlarging cysts ☐ Ruptured cyst ✅ Enlarging cysts. Weeks of dull, gradual aching = slow capsular stretch. A rupture is sudden, not gradual. "It feels like someone stabbed me in my back." — ☐ Enlarging kidney ☐ Ruptured cyst ☐ Kidney stone ✅ Ruptured cyst or a kidney stone — both cause abrupt, severe pain. Sort them out with the pattern: a stone is colicky and radiates to the groin and the patient cannot sit still; a rupture is more constant flank pain with new gross hematuria. Either way, assess for bleeding, hypotension, fever and urine output, and notify the provider.

Assessment finding Why does it happen? (say it in your own words) Hypertension Squeezed vessels → kidney thinks it is under-perfused → renin → RAAS → BP up Enlarged abdomen The kidneys themselves are the mass — cysts make them many times normal size Flank pain The renal capsule is being stretched from the inside Hematuria A cyst bleeds into the collecting system, or a stone scrapes the lining Kidney stones Stasis and distorted anatomy let minerals precipitate Progressive kidney failure Cysts physically replace working nephrons, and nephrons do not regenerate

entries.h: ⛔ STOP — your PKD patient's BP is 198/108. Just document it?
entries.t: YES / NO NO. Never document a pressure like this and walk away. Explain WHY. 198/108 is a hypertensive crisis in a patient who already has fragile renal vessels and an elevated risk of cerebral aneurysm. It is actively destroying nephrons and could cause a hemorrhagic stroke. Recheck manually, do a quick neuro and visual check, ask about headache/chest pain, look for missed antihypertensive doses, and notify the provider now.

1 — Monitor blood pressure (the parameter that can kill and the one that changes outcomes) 2 — Monitor renal labs (objective progression data + dangerous electrolytes) 3 — Assess pain (comfort, and a change in pattern signals an acute complication) 4 — Monitor daily weights (fluid status as GFR falls) 5 — Encourage a low-sodium diet (supports BP control — teaching) 6 — Teach home blood pressure monitoring (vital for the long haul, but the least urgent thing on this shift) Why is your top priority first? Because blood pressure is both the most immediately dangerous parameter and the one nursing intervention proven to slow progression to dialysis. Everything below it either measures the damage or supports the BP goal.

entries.h: 💊 Medication Connection — the provider prescribes an NSAID for chronic flank pain
entries.t: Should the nurse question this order? YES / NO YES — question it. Why? NSAIDs are nephrotoxic . They block prostaglandins that keep the afferent arteriole dilated, so renal blood flow drops — exactly what a PKD kidney cannot afford — and they raise blood pressure and cause sodium retention. In a patient whose whole treatment plan is "protect perfusion and control BP," an NSAID works against both. Acetaminophen is the preferred analgesic in kidney disease.

BP 188/104 · dull bilateral flank pain · abdominal fullness · creatinine 2.8 mg/dL · bloody urine Q1 — Which finding concerns you MOST? The BP of 188/104. It is the only finding that can cause an acute catastrophe (stroke, aneurysm rupture) and it is the one accelerating everything else. The flank pain, fullness and hematuria are expected in PKD. Q2 — Greatest long-term risk? Progression to end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplant — typically by age 50–60, and sooner if the hypertension stays uncontrolled. His creatinine of 2.8 says he is already well into CKD. Q3 — What intervention comes FIRST? Address the blood pressure — recheck it, review whether antihypertensives were taken, and notify the provider for orders. Because BP control is the intervention that protects the remaining nephrons and prevents an acute neurologic event. Q4 — What additional assessment shows whe

Disease Polycystic kidney disease ➜ Cause Inherited — usually autosomal dominant (50% risk to each child); an autosomal recessive infantile form also exists ➜ Patho Fluid-filled cysts form and enlarge, compressing nephrons and renal vessels → RAAS activation → hypertension → more nephron loss ➜ Findings Hypertension, bilateral flank pain, palpable enlarged kidneys and abdominal fullness, hematuria, stones, UTIs, nocturia, progressive fatigue, rising creatinine ➜ Priority care Blood pressure control (ACE inhibitor/ARB, low sodium, adherence), pain management without NSAIDs, monitor renal labs and weights, treat infections early, genetic counseling, prepare for renal replacement therapy ➜ Complications ESRD, hypertensive crisis, ruptured or infected cyst, cerebral berry aneurysm rupture, kidney stones, liver cysts NCLEX Pause — Which nursing intervention has the highest priority for a clie

entries.h: 🧠 Stop & Connect — look back at every renal disorder so far
entries.t: Disease What part of the kidney is affected? Highest nursing priority AKI Depends on the type — perfusion to the kidney (prerenal), the tubules themselves (intrarenal/ATN), or the outflow tract (postrenal) Monitor potassium and the ECG; track hourly urine output; manage fluids according to the phase (restrict in oliguric, replace in diuretic) CKD Progressive, permanent loss of nephrons throughout both kidneys Fluid and electrolyte control — hyperkalemia first; daily weights, BP control, dietary restrictions, protect the dialysis access Glomerulonephritis The glomerulus — inflamed filtering membrane Blood pressure control and fluid management; watch respiratory status for overload Nephrotic syndrome The glomerular membrane's permeability — it leaks protein Monitor edema and daily weight; watch for pulmonary edema, infection, and clots (DVT/PE) PKD The whole nephron mass — cysts physically

entries.h: Unit 18 · Renal Calculi — When Urine Stops Flowing 🪨
entries.t: A pebble in a garden hose. Water may still flow at first — but as it moves it scrapes, pressure builds behind it, and the pain becomes intense. 💙 Dr. K's tip: the pain is not the stone sitting in the kidney — it is the stone MOVING and blocking flow, making the ureter spasm. Build the Story 1 Urine becomes concentrated ➜ 2 Minerals begin to precipitate and crystallize ➜ 3 Stone forms ➜ 4 Stone moves into the ureter ➜ 5 Urine flow becomes obstructed / blocked ➜ 6 Pressure builds inside the kidney ➜ 7 Smooth muscle spasms — the ureter contracts violently trying to push the stone along ➜ 8 Severe colicky flank pain (renal colic) develops ⛔ Why do we push fluids? Dilute urine keeps minerals in solution so they cannot crystallize, and the volume helps flush an existing stone downstream. Target roughly 2.5–3 L/day unless the patient is fluid restricted — enough that the urine stays pale and clear. 🩺 What nursing interventions help a small stone pass? Generous fluids, ambulation (gravity and movement help it travel), effective pain control and antiemetics so the patient can stay hydrated and moving, warm/moist heat to the flank for spasm, and straining every void. Expect an alpha blocker such as tamsulosin to relax ureteral smooth muscle and speed passage.
