Choose one respiratory condition. Without looking at your notes, answer the five question groups below. Every condition on this page uses the same five groups — that repetition is the point. Group 1 What is happening in the body? Patho · lung changes · why symptoms ➜ Group 2 How do you know? Assessment · diagnostics · deterioration ➜ Group 3 How do you fix it? Priorities · meds · anticipated orders ➜ Group 4 Who is involved? The team ➜ Group 5 How can it get worse / be prevented? Complications · teaching

1. What is happening in the body? (patho, lung changes, why the symptoms) Model answer Airflow out of the lungs is chronically limited and not fully reversible — a mix of chronic bronchitis (inflamed, mucus-filled airways) and emphysema (destroyed alveoli). Lung change: airways narrow and collapse on exhalation, so air is trapped → residual volume rises and the chest hyperinflates Why dyspnea: because hyperinflated lungs flatten the diaphragm, so it can no longer generate an effective breath — accessory muscles take over Why the barrel chest: years of trapped air increase the anterior–posterior diameter Why CO₂ retention: trapped air is never exhaled, so CO₂ accumulates → chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic (renal) compensation — high PaCO₂ with a high HCO₂⁻ and a near-normal pH 2. How do you know? (expected findings, diagnostics, what says they are deteriorating) Model answer Expected findings: barrel chest, prolonged expiration, pursed-lip breathing, tripod position, accessory muscle use, chronic productive cough, wheezes or diminished breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion, clubbing, activity intolerance, weight loss Diagnostics: spirometry is definitive — a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70; ABG showing chronic respiratory acidosis; chest x-ray with hyperinflation and a flattened diaphragm; CBC that may show polycythemia from chronic hypoxemia Their usual

Emphysema sits under the COPD umbrella. Map what makes it different . 1. What is happening in the body? Model answer The alveolar walls are destroyed. Alveoli merge into large floppy sacs (bullae), which destroys surface area for gas exchange and destroys the elastic recoil that normally pushes air out. Why dyspnea is the main complaint: because without elastic recoil the patient must actively force air out, and with less alveolar surface, less oxygen crosses into the blood — so they work harder for a worse result Common cause: smoking; in a young patient with no smoking history think alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency 2. How do you know? Model answer Findings: thin, underweight, barrel chest with increased AP diameter, pursed-lip breathing, tripod position, minimal cough or sputum, hyperresonance on percussion, markedly diminished breath sounds, prolonged expiration Diagnostics: spirometry with a low FEV1/FVC and a raised residual volume, a reduced diffusing capacity (DLCO), CT/chest x-ray showing hyperinflation and bullae 🚨 Deterioration: increasing drowsiness — that is hypercarbia, and it is more worrying than the SpO₂. Also sudden sharp chest pain with unilateral absent breath sounds, which is a ruptured bulla causing pneumothorax. 3. How do you fix it? Model answer Priority: support ventilation, not just oxygenation — upright position, bronchodilator, controlled low-flow O₂ to

1. What is happening in the body? Model answer Three things at once, and all of them are reversible: bronchoconstriction (smooth muscle spasm), airway inflammation and edema, and thick mucus plugging Why the wheeze is on expiration: because airways narrow further as the chest deflates, so air is squeezed through narrowed tubes on the way out — and air is trapped behind the narrowing The key difference from COPD: asthma is episodic and reversible with a bronchodilator; COPD is chronic and only partly reversible 2. How do you know? Model answer Findings: expiratory wheezing, cough (often at night), chest tightness, dyspnea, prolonged expiratory phase, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, anxiety, and an inability to speak in full sentences when it is severe Diagnostics: spirometry showing obstruction that improves after a bronchodilator, peak expiratory flow rate compared with the patient's personal best, and ABGs in an acute attack Peak flow zones: Green 80–100% of personal best = good control. Yellow 50–79% = caution, use the rescue inhaler and follow the action plan. Red under 50% = emergency, rescue inhaler and get help. 🚨 The two findings that mean it is getting worse, not better: A silent chest — no wheeze because no air is moving. This is worse than loud wheezing. A "normalizing" or rising PaCO₂ — early in an attack they blow off CO₂ (respiratory alkalosis). A CO₂ that climbs

1. What is happening in the body? Model answer A clot — usually a DVT that broke off from a leg vein — lodges in the pulmonary circulation and blocks blood flow to part of the lung. Step 1 Clot blocks a pulmonary artery branch ➜ Step 2 That lung area is ventilated but not perfused — V/Q mismatch ➜ Step 3 Hypoxemia despite good breathing effort ➜ Step 4 Pulmonary pressure rises → right ventricular strain → shock Why the pain is sharp and worse on inspiration: infarcted lung tissue irritates the pleura — pleuritic pain Virchow's triad (why clots form): venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability — immobility, surgery, and cancer or estrogen therapy are the classic examples 2. How do you know? Model answer Findings: SUDDEN dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia, anxiety or a sense of impending doom, cough, hemoptysis, low-grade fever, and hypotension if the embolus is large Diagnostics: CT pulmonary angiography is the gold standard; D-dimer is useful mainly to rule PE out; V/Q scan when contrast is contraindicated (renal impairment, allergy); lower-extremity duplex ultrasound to find the source DVT; ABG usually shows respiratory alkalosis with hypoxemia; ECG most often shows sinus tachycardia 🚨 Deterioration: a rising respiratory rate, falling SpO₂ despite oxygen, falling blood pressure, JVD, and a change in level of consciousness — that is

1. What is happening in the body? Model answer Malignant cells grow in lung tissue, obstruct airways, invade nearby structures, and spread. Two families: non–small cell lung cancer (about 85%, includes adenocarcinoma and squamous cell — often treated surgically if caught early) and small cell lung cancer (aggressive, spreads early, treated with chemotherapy and radiation rather than surgery) Why the symptoms: a tumor obstructing an airway causes cough, wheeze, and post-obstructive pneumonia; invasion of vessels causes hemoptysis; pleural involvement causes pain and effusion; pressure on the laryngeal nerve causes hoarseness Biggest risk factor: tobacco smoke; then radon, asbestos and other occupational exposures, air pollution, and family history 2. How do you know? Model answer Findings: a persistent cough or a change in a chronic cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest or shoulder pain, hoarseness, recurrent pneumonia or bronchitis, unexplained weight loss and fatigue, and clubbing Diagnostics: chest x-ray and CT to find it, PET to stage it, and bronchoscopy or needle biopsy for the definitive tissue diagnosis; sputum cytology and mediastinoscopy for lymph node involvement Screening: annual low-dose CT for adults roughly 50–80 years old with a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years 🚨 Deterioration: facial and neck swelling with distended neck vein

1. What is happening in the body? (and what is the tube doing about it) Model answer Something has entered the pleural space that does not belong there — air (pneumothorax), blood (hemothorax), or fluid (effusion) — and it has destroyed the negative pressure that holds the lung open, so the lung collapses. The chest tube's job: remove the air or fluid and restore negative intrapleural pressure so the lung can re-expand Placement tells you what they are draining: a high/apical tube (about the 2nd–3rd intercostal space) removes air, because air rises; a low/basal tube (about the 5th–6th intercostal space, midaxillary) removes fluid or blood, because fluid settles 2. How do you know? (what is normal in the drainage system, and what is not) Model answer What you see Expected ✅ Report / act ❌ Water-seal chamber Tidaling — the fluid level rises and falls with breathing. Intermittent bubbling is expected with a pneumothorax as trapped air escapes. CONTINUOUS bubbling = an air leak in the system. Check all connections first, then work toward the patient. Tidaling stops If the patient is comfortable and breath sounds are back — the lung has re-expanded. If the patient is dyspneic — the tubing is kinked, clamped, obstructed, or dependent-looped. Assess the patient, not just the box. Suction chamber (wet) Gentle continuous bubbling — that is the suction working, not an air leak. No bubbli

1. What is happening in the body? (why they need it, and what the machine changes) Model answer The patient cannot maintain adequate oxygenation, ventilation, or a patent airway on their own. Indications: hypoxemic respiratory failure, hypercarbic respiratory failure (a rising PaCO₂ with a falling pH), inability to protect the airway, apnea, and severe work of breathing that is exhausting them The key physiologic change: normal breathing pulls air in with NEGATIVE pressure; a ventilator pushes air in with POSITIVE pressure. Positive pressure in the chest reduces venous return, so it can lower cardiac output and blood pressure — especially with high PEEP. Common settings: FiO₂ (percent oxygen), tidal volume (roughly 6–8 mL/kg of ideal body weight, and 6 mL/kg in ARDS to prevent volutrauma), respiratory rate, and PEEP (usually starting around 5 cm H₂O) which holds alveoli open at the end of exhalation 2. How do you know? (confirming placement, expected findings, alarms) Model answer Confirming ET tube placement: continuous waveform capnography (ETCO₂) plus equal bilateral breath sounds and symmetric chest rise; a chest x-ray is the definitive confirmation. Note and document the centimeter marking at the lips every shift so you know if it migrates. If breath sounds are heard only on the right: the tube has slipped into the right mainstem bronchus — notify the provider so it can be

Instead of broad questions, try prompts such as: "Teach me COPD as if I am preparing for NCLEX." · "Compare asthma, COPD, and emphysema in a table." · "Create five ATI-style questions about pulmonary embolism with rationales." · "Walk me through a mechanical ventilation case study." · "Explain hypercarbia using patient examples." · "Help me distinguish assessment findings that require intervention versus continued assessment."

Before selecting an answer, run these in order. Same order, every question. Step 1 What is the question asking? Assessment · Intervention · Priority · Teaching · Evaluation ➜ Step 2 What abnormal cues stand out? ➜ Step 3 Is this an A irway, B reathing, or C irculation problem? ➜ Step 4 Do I have enough to act, or do I need more assessment? ➜ Step 5 Eliminate distractors Eliminate distractors by asking Does this answer delay treatment ? Does this answer address the priority problem ? Is this intervention appropriate for the current situation ? Model answer: how do I actually tell "assess more" from "act now"? Model answer Assess further when… Intervene NOW when… The cue is vague or you cannot name the problem yet — "reports feeling tired," "states the pain is different," a single borderline value in a stable patient. The cue names a threat to airway, breathing, or circulation — a silent chest, SpO₂ 86%, new confusion, a respiratory rate climbing 20 → 32, absent breath sounds on one side. Nothing will get worse in the next few minutes if you gather more data. Waiting costs oxygen or perfusion. Then the answer is the action that opens the airway or improves ventilation — not a test, not documentation. Diagnostics never beat interventions when the patient is decompensating. ABGs, x-rays, and charting all delay treatment.

Answer all four before you open any reveal. The Answer Key and Rationales is attached to each question — correct answer plus why every distractor is wrong. 1. A nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first? A client with COPD who reports fatigue after walking to the bathroom. A client with asthma requesting the next scheduled nebulizer treatment. A client with pulmonary embolism whose respiratory rate increased from 20/min to 32/min during the last hour. A client with pneumonia whose temperature increased from 37.6°C to 38.0°C. Show the answer Correct: C. The respiratory rate jumped 12 breaths in an hour in a client who already has a clot obstructing pulmonary blood flow. That is a trend, not a number, and it says the client is deteriorating toward respiratory failure or right heart strain. A — Fatigue with exertion is expected in COPD; it is the disease behaving normally. B — A routine scheduled medication request. Important, but nobody is unstable. D — A 0.4°C rise is mild and expected with pneumonia; there is no sign of acute instability. When a question gives you two numbers, it is asking about the trend. 2. A client with emphysema has an oxygen saturation of 91% while receiving prescribed oxygen therapy. During reassessment, the client becomes increasingly difficult to arouse. Which nursing action is most appropriate? Encourage pursed-l

entries.h: 🚨 Case Study 1 · Clinical Judgment Measurement Model
entries.t: A 67-year-old client presents with: Sudden onset shortness of breath Sharp chest pain that worsens with inspiration Heart rate 124/min · Respiratory rate 34/min Oxygen saturation 86% on room air Hip replacement surgery 10 days ago Blood-streaked sputum Recognize Cues — What findings are most concerning? Model answer Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia at 124, tachypnea at 34, hypoxemia at 86% on room air, hemoptysis, and recent orthopedic surgery with the immobility that follows it. The two that carry the most weight: SpO₂ 86% on room air (a direct oxygenation failure) and the word "sudden" combined with hip surgery 10 days ago (the risk factor that names the diagnosis). Analyze Cues — What diagnosis best explains the presentation? Model answer Pulmonary embolism , most likely from a DVT that formed in the operative leg during postoperative immobility. Sudden onset, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, and hemoptysis together are the textbook picture, and orthopedic surgery is a top-tier risk factor. Why not pneumonia? Pneumonia builds over days with fever, productive purulent sputum, and crackles — it is not sudden. Why not MI? MI pain is usually pressure that does not change with breathing, and it does not produce blood-streaked sputum. Prioritize Hypotheses — What is your greatest concern? Model answer Impaired oxygenation from obstruction of pulmonary blood

entries.h: Case Study 2 · Clinical Judgment Measurement Model
entries.t: A 72-year-old client with severe emphysema presents with: Respiratory rate 30/min Oxygen saturation 90% on prescribed oxygen Barrel chest · Accessory muscle use · Diminished breath sounds Increasing drowsiness Recognize Cues Model answer Barrel chest, diminished breath sounds, accessory muscle use, respiratory rate 30, and — the one that changed — increasing drowsiness. Which are chronic and which are new? Barrel chest is chronic and expected. Diminished breath sounds and accessory muscle use are baseline-plus. The increasing drowsiness is NEW, and new is what you act on. Analyze Cues Model answer The new drowsiness means worsening carbon dioxide retention (hypercarbia) — the client is breathing fast but shallowly and moving very little air, so CO₂ builds up. High CO₂ is a sedative to the brain, which is why they get sleepy. The SpO₂ of 90% is normal for this client and is falsely reassuring: oxygenation is adequate while ventilation is failing. SpO₂ measures oxygenation. It tells you nothing about CO₂. Only an ABG and the client's mental status do. Prioritize Hypotheses Model answer Impending respiratory failure from hypercarbia — respiratory acidosis with a falling pH, progressing to obtundation, apnea, and the need for intubation if nothing changes. Generate Solutions Model answer Support ventilation as well as oxygenation, reassess frequently, and notify the provider of the

Before the exam, ask yourself — and answer out loud, not in your head: Can I explain the pathophysiology without looking at my notes? Can I recognize this disease from assessment findings alone? Can I identify which finding is most concerning? Can I distinguish when NCLEX wants another assessment versus immediate intervention? Can I explain why the correct answer is right and why every distractor is wrong? Model answer: what does "good enough" sound like for each of these? Model answer Patho: You can say the chain out loud — cause → lung change → symptom — in about three sentences without a pause. Recognize from findings: Given only "sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, recent surgery," you say PE before you finish reading. Most concerning finding: You pick the one that CHANGED and the one that threatens airway, breathing, or circulation — not the ugliest number. Assess vs. act: You can state the rule: if waiting costs oxygen or perfusion, act; if the cue is vague and nothing gets worse in the next few minutes, gather more data. Rationales: For each wrong option you can name its specific flaw — delays treatment, treats the wrong problem, or is right but not first. 🤖 After this packet, use ATI Engage Dynamic Quizzing and Claire to generate more questions on anything you had to peek at.

Trend beats number. RR 20 → 32 in an hour is the sicker client, even if someone else's single value looks worse. Mental status beats pulse ox in COPD/emphysema. New drowsiness = CO₂ retention and impending respiratory failure . Target SpO₂ in COPD is 88–92% . Do not crank the oxygen to fix drowsiness. A silent chest in asthma is worse than a loud wheeze — no air is moving . "Sudden" dyspnea after surgery or immobility = pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise . Chest tube: continuous bubbling in the water seal = air leak; tube out of the chest = sterile dressing taped on three sides; tube off the system = end into sterile water . Never clamp routinely. Ventilator: HIGH pressure = obstruction (suction, unkink); LOW pressure = leak or disconnect (trace the circuit) . In distress → bag them with 100% O₂ and think DOPE . Interventions beat diagnostics when the patient is decompensating. ABGs, x-rays, and charting all delay treatment.
